Probationary Period Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out the probationary period every new employee serves, and how it is reviewed and confirmed. It applies to every new starter, and to any existing employee moving into a new role that Alderbridge treats as requiring a fresh probationary assessment.

Policy statement

Probation is a genuine, two-way assessment period: Alderbridge assesses whether the new starter is settling well and meeting the role's requirements, and the new starter assesses whether the role and Alderbridge are right for them, with support and honest feedback flowing in both directions throughout.

Definitions

**Probationary period** the standard 6-month period from an employee's start date during which suitability is formally assessed. **Extension** an additional period, up to 3 months, added where more time is genuinely needed to reach a fair decision. **Probation review** a scheduled formal conversation reviewing progress against the role's requirements.

Roles and responsibilities

**The line manager** holds regular informal check-ins and every formal review, raising any concern as soon as it arises rather than saving it for a scheduled review. **HR** confirms the outcome of each formal review in writing and advises on any complex case. **The new starter** engages openly with feedback and raises any concern about their own induction or support.

The probationary period runs for 6 months from the start date, extendable by up to a further 3 months at the registered manager's discretion where more time is needed.

Formal review meetings are held at 6 weeks, 3 months and 5 months, each recorded in writing.

Any conduct, capability or attendance concern is raised with the employee as soon as it arises, not held back until the next scheduled review.

Successful completion of probation is confirmed to the employee in writing, normally by the end of the 6-month period.

Training and competency

Managers conducting probation reviews complete training on giving fair, constructive feedback and documenting a review properly.

Probation for an internal transfer

An employee moving internally into a different role completes a shorter, 3-month probationary period focused specifically on the new role's distinct requirements, recognising their already-established good standing at Alderbridge while still confirming genuine suitability for the specific new responsibilities involved, which may differ materially from their previous role even at the same organisation.

Probation outcomes short of full confirmation or termination

Occasionally a review finds performance genuinely mixed rather than clearly satisfactory or unsatisfactory; in this situation the registered manager may agree a short, specific extension with clear, written improvement expectations rather than being forced into a binary confirm-or-end decision when the fairer, more accurate assessment is that more time and clearer expectations are what is actually needed.

The role of HR as a genuine safeguard for fairness

HR reviews every proposed non-confirmation decision before it is communicated to the employee, checking that concerns were raised in good time, that support was genuinely offered where appropriate, and that the decision is well documented and consistent with how similar situations have been handled elsewhere, so that a probation decision is never simply one manager's unreviewed, unilateral judgement, however experienced that manager may be.

Disciplinary hearings are deliberately held away from the employee's own immediate workplace wherever practicable — for the four care homes and Willow Bank, this typically means using a meeting room at Central Support Office or, where travel is impractical, a private room at a nearby site rather than the employee's own site, to reduce the risk of the hearing itself becoming visible to colleagues or people supported.

Extended worked example: a capability-shaped conduct concern

A worked example illustrates the boundary between conduct and capability. A relatively new care worker at Riverside House has made three separate documentation errors on care records within two months, none individually serious but forming a pattern. Rather than moving straight to a formal disciplinary hearing, the line manager first considers whether this looks like unwillingness (a conduct matter) or a genuine skills gap (a capability matter) — in this example, the employee's own account and the line manager's review of their induction records show they were never given adequate protected time to complete the documentation training module properly. Induction Buddy Scheme Guidance

*Supersedes the version effective 1 September 2025. 'Should' becomes 'must' — the buddy assignment is no longer discretionary.*

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the induction buddy scheme offered to a new starter at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every new starter across every site.

Policy statement

New starters must be assigned an experienced buddy for their first 4 weeks — no longer discretionary — giving every new starter an approachable, informal point of contact alongside their formal induction programme.

Definitions

**Buddy** an experienced staff member paired with a new starter to offer informal support and answer day-to-day questions. **Buddy period** the first 4 weeks of a new starter's employment, during which the buddy pairing is now mandatory.

1. Identify a suitable experienced staff member as a buddy before the new starter's first day; this assignment is now mandatory rather than discretionary as under the previous version.
2. Introduce the buddy to the new starter on their first day, explaining the buddy's role as an informal, approachable point of contact.
3. Check in with both the buddy and the new starter partway through the 4-week period to see how the pairing is working.
4. Extend the buddy period beyond 4 weeks where both the buddy and new starter feel this would be helpful.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where no suitable experienced staff member is available at a small site, the registered manager arranges a buddy from a neighbouring site for informal telephone or message support; since assignment is now mandatory, the absence of an obvious on-site buddy is no longer treated as grounds to skip the scheme entirely.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the New Starter Induction Programme Outline (the formal induction this scheme complements) and the Staff Supervision and Appraisal Policy (the more formal line management relationship this scheme sits alongside).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates how the amber trigger point is used supportively rather than punitively. A care worker at Harbour View reaches the amber trigger point after three short, apparently unconnected absences (a stomach bug, a migraine, and a dental abscess) within eight months. At the return-to-work discussion following the third absence, the line manager raises the pattern gently, asks whether anything at work might be contributing, and learns that recent long shifts without an adequate break have been making the employee's migraines worse. Rather than treating the trigger as itself the problem, the line manager and employee agree a shift-length adjustment for a trial period, and no formal absence review meeting is needed, because the amber conversation itself surfaced and addressed the underlying issue — exactly the outcome this policy is designed to produce at that stage.

Extended worked example: a sustained absence with an uncertain return date

A second worked example addresses the harder case of long-term sickness absence. An employee at Oakfield Lodge has been absent for 6 weeks following surgery, with the GP's fit note indicating an uncertain return date. HR arranges an occupational health referral at 4 weeks, per the sustained trigger point, and the resulting report suggests a phased return over 4 weeks with modified duties (no manual handling) would be achievable from week 8. The registered manager agrees this phased return plan with the employee, reviewing it fortnightly and adjusting the pace if the employee's own recovery runs ahead of or behind the initial estimate, rather than treating the occupational health report as a fixed, unchangeable timetable regardless of how the employee is actually progressing.

What a formal absence review meeting actually covers

A formal absence review meeting triggered at the red level is a genuinely two-way conversation, not a predetermined disciplinary step: it reviews the specific pattern openly, explores whether an underlying cause (health, workplace factors, or personal circumstances) can be identified and addressed, considers whether occupational health input would help, and only where a pattern is not disability-related and shows no sign of improving despite support does it begin to move toward considering whether continued employment in the current role remains sustainable — a possibility discussed transparently rather than left unspoken while informally already decided.

Confidentiality of health information disclosed during absence management

Any health information an employee shares as part of a return-to-work discussion or a formal absence review is treated as confidential, shared only with those who genuinely need to know (for example, HR and, where a reasonable adjustment is agreed, the employee's own line manager) rather than discussed more widely, and an employee is never expected to disclose more clinical detail than they are comfortable sharing beyond what a fit note or occupational health report already confirms.

Absence during a probationary period

A probationary employee's absence is monitored against the same trigger points, but the shorter probationary window means HR and the line manager review any absence pattern more promptly, since a genuine, sustained concern about attendance reliability is relevant to the eventual probation confirmation decision under the Probationary Period Policy, discussed openly with the employee rather than left unaddressed until the probation end date arrives.

Closing note on tone

Every conversation this policy describes — a return-to-work discussion, an absence review, a trigger-point escalation — is expected to be conducted with genuine warmth and curiosity about what is actually going on for the employee, since a policy applied correctly but coldly achieves compliance without achieving the actual purpose this policy exists for, which is a workplace where people feel able to be honest about being unwell and supported back when they are ready.

Governance and reporting

HR reviews every disciplinary outcome quarterly across all sites, specifically checking for consistency in how similar conduct has been treated at different sites, and reports a summarised, anonymised picture to the Chief Executive twice a year.

Appendix: the staged process at a glance

This appendix summarises the staged process described above for quick reference. An informal conversation, recorded briefly, is the starting point for most minor concerns. A first written warning follows a formal hearing where informal action has not resolved a genuine concern, and stays live for 6 months. A final written warning follows a further offence during that period, or a sufficiently serious first offence, and stays live for 12 months. Dismissal with notice may follow a further offence while a final warning is live. Dismissal without notice may follow a single act of gross misconduct, at any stage, without needing to pass through the earlier stages first. An appeal is available at every formal stage, heard by a manager not previously involved, and its outcome is final within Alderbridge's own internal process, though an employee retains whatever external legal rights apply regardless of the outcome of an internal appeal.

Investigating fairly

An investigation gathers evidence objectively, seeking information that might support the employee's account as diligently as information that might support the allegation, and is completed by someone with no personal involvement in the matter and, wherever practicable, no direct reporting line to the employee concerned, so that both the fact and the appearance of a fair, independent process are preserved.

Leave and absence

Annual leave entitlement is set out in each employee's own contract and requested through the standard leave request process; sickness absence is reported to the registered manager as early as possible on the first day of absence, now with a wellbeing check-in offered as part of the return-to-work process.

Standards of conduct

Every employee is expected to treat a resident, colleague, and visitor with dignity and respect at all times, to act within the boundaries of their own training and competence, and to raise a concern honestly rather than conceal it.

Health and safety responsibilities

Every employee has a personal responsibility to work safely, to report a hazard or near-miss promptly, and to follow the specific safety procedure relevant to their role; the Health and Safety Policy (Full Manual) sets out the complete framework.

Safeguarding responsibilities

Every employee has a personal responsibility to report a safeguarding concern immediately to their registered manager, following the Adult Safeguarding Policy.

Equality, diversity and inclusion

Alderbridge is committed to treating every employee and resident fairly regardless of a protected characteristic; a concern about discrimination or unfair treatment is raised with Human Resources and taken seriously.

Confidentiality and data protection

An employee has access to confidential information about a resident, a colleague, or Alderbridge's own business in the course of their role; this information is shared only on a need-to-know basis and never disclosed outside of work.

Use of Alderbridge equipment and systems

Alderbridge equipment is provided for legitimate work purposes; reasonable personal use of a shared computer is generally acceptable where it does not interfere with work or breach confidentiality.

Grievance and dispute resolution

Where an employee has a concern about their treatment at work, they are encouraged to raise it informally with their registered manager in the first instance; where this does not resolve the matter, the formal Grievance Procedure sets out the full process.

Training and development

Every employee completes mandatory training relevant to their role as part of induction and on an ongoing refresher basis; a development conversation takes place at least annually as part of the appraisal process.

Uniform and appearance

Where a role requires a uniform, this is provided by Alderbridge and is expected to be worn clean and in good repair; general appearance standards are set out in the Dress and Appearance Guidance.

Purpose and scope

Policy statement

Definitions

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains how a staff member's competency in a core or specialist care task is assessed and recorded at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every care role.

Policy statement

A staff member's competency is assessed against the novice, competent and expert framework with annual re-validation, now incorporating a peer-observation element alongside senior sign-off, with each staff member maintaining their own formal competency portfolio.

Definitions

**Competency framework** the structured levels a staff member's task ability is assessed against. **Peer observation** the new element, introduced in this version, where a competent or expert colleague also contributes an observation alongside the senior staff member's own assessment. **Competency portfolio** the new formal record, introduced in this version, that each staff member maintains themselves, consolidating their own assessment, re-validation and peer observation history.

Roles and responsibilities

**A senior staff member** signs off competency progression and annual re-validation, now informed by peer observation input. **A peer observer**, a new role introduced in this version, provides a structured observation contributing to a colleague's assessment. **The staff member** maintains their own competency portfolio, keeping it current and available for review.

Where the investigation finds a case to answer, the employee is invited in writing to a formal hearing, given at least 2 working days' notice, told the specific allegation, and provided with the investigation evidence in advance.

The employee has the right to be accompanied at the hearing by a trade union representative or a work colleague of their choice.

At the hearing, the employee is given a full opportunity to respond to the allegation, ask questions, and present their own evidence before any decision is reached.

A decision is confirmed in writing within 5 working days of the hearing wherever possible, giving reasons and, where a sanction is applied, its duration and the right of appeal.

The first formal stage is normally a first written warning, live for 6 months; a further offence within that period, or a sufficiently serious first offence, may move directly to a final written warning, live for 12 months.

A further offence while a final written warning is live may result in dismissal with notice, or without notice if the conduct amounts to gross misconduct.

An employee may appeal any formal outcome in writing within 10 working days, to a manager not previously involved, whose decision is final within Alderbridge's own internal process.

Gross misconduct examples

Examples of gross misconduct include theft, physical violence, being under the influence of drugs or alcohol on duty, gross negligence causing serious harm to a person supported, serious breach of the Safe Administration of Medication Policy or Controlled Drugs Procedure, and serious or repeated breach of confidentiality. This is not an exhaustive list; the Employee Handbook's Section 4 gives further illustrative examples, and a matter not listed here may still be treated as gross misconduct where its seriousness genuinely warrants it.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where an allegation also raises a safeguarding concern, the Safeguarding Adults Policy and Allegations Against Staff Procedure run in parallel with this procedure; a decision to suspend on full pay pending investigation is taken on safeguarding grounds and is never treated as itself a disciplinary sanction or a presumption of guilt.

Local and regional variations

No local or regional variation applies to this procedure — disciplinary process is deliberately standardised across all five sites and Central Support Office to ensure consistent, fair treatment regardless of location.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates how the amber trigger point is used supportively rather than punitively. A care worker at Harbour View reaches the amber trigger point after three short, apparently unconnected absences (a stomach bug, a migraine, and a dental abscess) within eight months. At the return-to-work discussion following the third absence, the line manager raises the pattern gently, asks whether anything at work might be contributing, and learns that recent long shifts without an adequate break have been making the employee's migraines worse. Rather than treating the trigger as itself the problem, the line manager and employee agree a shift-length adjustment for a trial period, and no formal absence review meeting is needed, because the amber conversation itself surfaced and addressed the underlying issue — exactly the outcome this policy is designed to produce at that stage.

Extended worked example: a sustained absence with an uncertain return date

A second worked example addresses the harder case of long-term sickness absence. An employee at Oakfield Lodge has been absent for 6 weeks following surgery, with the GP's fit note indicating an uncertain return date. HR arranges an occupational health referral at 4 weeks, per the sustained trigger point, and the resulting report suggests a phased return over 4 weeks with modified duties (no manual handling) would be achievable from week 8. The registered manager agrees this phased return plan with the employee, reviewing it fortnightly and adjusting the pace if the employee's own recovery runs ahead of or behind the initial estimate, rather than treating the occupational health report as a fixed, unchangeable timetable regardless of how the employee is actually progressing.

Probationary Period Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out the probationary period every new employee serves, and how it is reviewed and confirmed. It applies to every new starter, and to any existing employee moving into a new role that Alderbridge treats as requiring a fresh probationary assessment.

Policy statement

Probation is a genuine, two-way assessment period: Alderbridge assesses whether the new starter is settling well and meeting the role's requirements, and the new starter assesses whether the role and Alderbridge are right for them, with support and honest feedback flowing in both directions throughout.

Definitions

**Probationary period** the standard 6-month period from an employee's start date during which suitability is formally assessed. **Extension** an additional period, up to 3 months, added where more time is genuinely needed to reach a fair decision. **Probation review** a scheduled formal conversation reviewing progress against the role's requirements.

Roles and responsibilities

**The line manager** holds regular informal check-ins and every formal review, raising any concern as soon as it arises rather than saving it for a scheduled review. **HR** confirms the outcome of each formal review in writing and advises on any complex case. **The new starter** engages openly with feedback and raises any concern about their own induction or support.

The probationary period runs for 6 months from the start date, extendable by up to a further 3 months at the registered manager's discretion where more time is needed.

Formal review meetings are held at 6 weeks, 3 months and 5 months, each recorded in writing.

Any conduct, capability or attendance concern is raised with the employee as soon as it arises, not held back until the next scheduled review.

Successful completion of probation is confirmed to the employee in writing, normally by the end of the 6-month period.

The line manager therefore addresses this initially through additional supervised practice and a revised, individual learning plan rather than the formal disciplinary process, while recording clearly why that judgement was made, so that if the same pattern continues despite that support, the earlier informal period is not treated as if it never happened.

Probation for an internal transfer

Occasionally a review finds performance genuinely mixed rather than clearly satisfactory or unsatisfactory; in this situation the registered manager may agree a short, specific extension with clear, written improvement expectations rather than being forced into a binary confirm-or-end decision when the fairer, more accurate assessment is that more time and clearer expectations are what is actually needed.

Long Service Recognition Scheme

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains how Alderbridge Care Group recognises a staff member's long service. It applies
to every permanent member of staff across every site.

Policy statement

Long service is recognised meaningfully at defined milestones, reflecting the genuine value of experienced
staff who have chosen to build their career at Alderbridge.

Definitions

**Milestone year** a service anniversary of 5, 10, 15 or 20 years, at which a specific recognition is given.
**Continuous service** service counted without a break exceeding the threshold set out in the Staff
Handbook, used to determine milestone eligibility.

1. HR identifies an upcoming milestone anniversary from payroll records and notifies the site three months
in advance.

2. Present recognition at a team meeting or similar site event, marking the milestone visibly rather than
only administratively.

3. Award a certificate at every milestone, with an additional day of annual leave awarded from the 10-year
milestone onward and a cash award from the 15-year milestone onward.

4. Record the recognition given in the staff member's personnel file.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a staff member has had a single approved career break (such as extended parental leave) that
would otherwise interrupt continuous service, the registered manager may request HR treat this as
continuous for scheme purposes, consistent with the Staff Handbook's continuous service definition.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the Staff Benefits Guidance (the wider set of benefits this scheme sits
alongside) and the Annual Leave Policy (governing how the milestone leave day is added and used).

Staff Reference Request Procedure

Supersedes the version effective 1 June 2025. Response time tightened from 10 to 5 working days.

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group responds to a reference request for a current or
former staff member. It applies to every reference request received by HR.

Policy statement

HR provides a factual reference confirming dates of employment and job title within 5 working days of a
request, tightened from the previous 10 working days, giving a former or current staff member a faster,
reliable response supporting their next step.

Definitions

**Factual reference** a reference limited to objective facts such as dates of employment and job title, as
distinct from a subjective opinion-based reference. **Reference request** a request received in writing
from a prospective employer or other authorised party, with the staff member's consent where required.

Roles and responsibilities

**HR** processes every reference request and issues the factual reference within the tightened
5-working-day timeframe. **The staff member's line manager** is not the point of contact for a formal
reference request, which is handled centrally by HR to ensure consistency. **The requesting party**
provides sufficient detail, including the staff member's consent where required, for HR to process the
request.

1. Log every reference request on receipt, confirming it includes sufficient detail and any required consent.

2. Issue a factual reference confirming dates of employment and job title within 5 working days of the
request being received, a tightening from the previous 10-working-day standard.

3. Limit the reference to factual, objective information; a subjective opinion on the staff member's
performance or conduct is not included.

4. Direct a request for a fuller, opinion-based reference to the registered manager, who decides whether
and how to respond to that specific, different type of request.

Induction Buddy Scheme Guidance

*Supersedes the version effective 1 September 2025. 'Should' becomes 'must' — the buddy assignment is no longer discretionary.*

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the induction buddy scheme offered to a new starter at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every new starter across every site.

Policy statement

New starters must be assigned an experienced buddy for their first 4 weeks — no longer discretionary — giving every new starter an approachable, informal point of contact alongside their formal induction programme.

Definitions

**Buddy** an experienced staff member paired with a new starter to offer informal support and answer day-to-day questions. **Buddy period** the first 4 weeks of a new starter's employment, during which the buddy pairing is now mandatory.

1. Identify a suitable experienced staff member as a buddy before the new starter's first day; this assignment is now mandatory rather than discretionary as under the previous version.
2. Introduce the buddy to the new starter on their first day, explaining the buddy's role as an informal, approachable point of contact.
3. Check in with both the buddy and the new starter partway through the 4-week period to see how the pairing is working.
4. Extend the buddy period beyond 4 weeks where both the buddy and new starter feel this would be helpful.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where no suitable experienced staff member is available at a small site, the registered manager arranges a buddy from a neighbouring site for informal telephone or message support; since assignment is now mandatory, the absence of an obvious on-site buddy is no longer treated as grounds to skip the scheme entirely.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the New Starter Induction Programme Outline (the formal induction this scheme complements) and the Staff Supervision and Appraisal Policy (the more formal line management relationship this scheme sits alongside).

A worked example illustrates the immutable backup's purpose. During a simulated ransomware exercise,
IT finds that standard, writable backups from the preceding week would themselves have been encrypted
alongside the primary system in a genuine attack of this type; the immutable, air-gapped copy remains
untouched and unencrypted, providing the actual recovery source the exercise confirms would be needed

Frequently asked questions

**Why was an immutable backup added when the 3-2-1 principle already existed?** A review found that a
sophisticated ransomware attack can specifically target and encrypt a standard backup alongside the
primary system if both are reachable from the same compromised network; an immutable, air-gapped copy
cannot be altered even in that scenario. **What is the difference between RTO and RPO?** RTO is how
quickly a system is restored; RPO is how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable — a
nightly-backed-up system has an RPO of roughly 24 hours since up to a day's data could be lost if the
incident occurs just before that night's backup.

Training and competency

building on the existing monthly test restoration training.

monthly, reporting to the Board quarterly.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out the probationary period every new employee serves, and how it is reviewed and confirmed. It applies to every new starter, and to any existing employee moving into a new role that Alderbridge treats as requiring a fresh probationary assessment.

Policy statement

Probation is a genuine, two-way assessment period: Alderbridge assesses whether the new starter is settling well and meeting the role's requirements, and the new starter assesses whether the role and Alderbridge are right for them, with support and honest feedback flowing in both directions throughout.

Definitions

**Probationary period** the standard 6-month period from an employee's start date during which suitability is formally assessed. **Extension** an additional period, up to 3 months, added where more time is genuinely needed to reach a fair decision. **Probation review** a scheduled formal conversation reviewing progress against the role's requirements.

Roles and responsibilities

**The line manager** holds regular informal check-ins and every formal review, raising any concern as soon as it arises rather than saving it for a scheduled review. **HR** confirms the outcome of each formal review in writing and advises on any complex case. **The new starter** engages openly with feedback and raises any concern about their own induction or support.

The probationary period runs for 6 months from the start date, extendable by up to a further 3 months at the registered manager's discretion where more time is needed.

Formal review meetings are held at 6 weeks, 3 months and 5 months, each recorded in writing.

Any conduct, capability or attendance concern is raised with the employee as soon as it arises, not held back until the next scheduled review.

Probation for an internal transfer

Worked example

A worked example illustrates how the amber trigger point is used supportively rather than punitively. A care worker at Harbour View reaches the amber trigger point after three short, apparently unconnected absences (a stomach bug, a migraine, and a dental abscess) within eight months. At the return-to-work discussion following the third absence, the line manager raises the pattern gently, asks whether anything at work might be contributing, and learns that recent long shifts without an adequate break have been making the employee's migraines worse. Rather than treating the trigger as itself the problem, the line manager and employee agree a shift-length adjustment for a trial period, and no formal absence review meeting is needed, because the amber conversation itself surfaced and addressed the underlying issue — exactly the outcome this policy is designed to produce at that stage.

Extended worked example: a sustained absence with an uncertain return date

A second worked example addresses the harder case of long-term sickness absence. An employee at Oakfield Lodge has been absent for 6 weeks following surgery, with the GP's fit note indicating an uncertain return date. HR arranges an occupational health referral at 4 weeks, per the sustained trigger point, and the resulting report suggests a phased return over 4 weeks with modified duties (no manual handling) would be achievable from week 8. The registered manager agrees this phased return plan with the employee, reviewing it fortnightly and adjusting the pace if the employee's own recovery runs ahead of or behind the initial estimate, rather than treating the occupational health report as a fixed, unchangeable timetable regardless of how the employee is actually progressing.

Induction Buddy Scheme Guidance

*Supersedes the version effective 1 September 2025. 'Should' becomes 'must' — the buddy assignment is no longer discretionary.*

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the induction buddy scheme offered to a new starter at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every new starter across every site.

Policy statement

New starters must be assigned an experienced buddy for their first 4 weeks — no longer discretionary — giving every new starter an approachable, informal point of contact alongside their formal induction programme.

Definitions

**Buddy** an experienced staff member paired with a new starter to offer informal support and answer day-to-day questions. **Buddy period** the first 4 weeks of a new starter's employment, during which the buddy pairing is now mandatory.

1. Identify a suitable experienced staff member as a buddy before the new starter's first day; this assignment is now mandatory rather than discretionary as under the previous version.
2. Introduce the buddy to the new starter on their first day, explaining the buddy's role as an informal, approachable point of contact.
3. Check in with both the buddy and the new starter partway through the 4-week period to see how the pairing is working.
4. Extend the buddy period beyond 4 weeks where both the buddy and new starter feel this would be helpful.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where no suitable experienced staff member is available at a small site, the registered manager arranges a buddy from a neighbouring site for informal telephone or message support; since assignment is now mandatory, the absence of an obvious on-site buddy is no longer treated as grounds to skip the scheme entirely.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the New Starter Induction Programme Outline (the formal induction this scheme complements) and the Staff Supervision and Appraisal Policy (the more formal line management relationship this scheme sits alongside).

Matching safeguarding training to a role's actual resident contact keeps the training genuinely relevant, and this guidance exists to make that matching consistent across every site.

Probationary Period Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out the probationary period every new employee serves, and how it is reviewed and confirmed. It applies to every new starter, and to any existing employee moving into a new role that Alderbridge treats as requiring a fresh probationary assessment.

Policy statement

Probation is a genuine, two-way assessment period: Alderbridge assesses whether the new starter is settling well and meeting the role's requirements, and the new starter assesses whether the role and Alderbridge are right for them, with support and honest feedback flowing in both directions throughout.

Definitions

**Probationary period** the standard 6-month period from an employee's start date during which suitability is formally assessed. **Extension** an additional period, up to 3 months, added where more time is genuinely needed to reach a fair decision. **Probation review** a scheduled formal conversation reviewing progress against the role's requirements.

Roles and responsibilities

**The line manager** holds regular informal check-ins and every formal review, raising any concern as soon as it arises rather than saving it for a scheduled review. **HR** confirms the outcome of each formal review in writing and advises on any complex case. **The new starter** engages openly with feedback and raises any concern about their own induction or support.

The probationary period runs for 6 months from the start date, extendable by up to a further 3 months at the registered manager's discretion where more time is needed.

Formal review meetings are held at 6 weeks, 3 months and 5 months, each recorded in writing.

Any conduct, capability or attendance concern is raised with the employee as soon as it arises, not held back until the next scheduled review.

Successful completion of probation is confirmed to the employee in writing, normally by the end of the 6-month period.

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the induction buddy scheme offered to a new starter at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every new starter across every site.

Policy statement

New starters must be assigned an experienced buddy for their first 4 weeks — no longer discretionary — giving every new starter an approachable, informal point of contact alongside their formal induction programme.

Definitions

**Buddy** an experienced staff member paired with a new starter to offer informal support and answer day-to-day questions. **Buddy period** the first 4 weeks of a new starter's employment, during which the buddy pairing is now mandatory.

1. Identify a suitable experienced staff member as a buddy before the new starter's first day; this assignment is now mandatory rather than discretionary as under the previous version.
2. Introduce the buddy to the new starter on their first day, explaining the buddy's role as an informal, approachable point of contact.
3. Check in with both the buddy and the new starter partway through the 4-week period to see how the pairing is working.
4. Extend the buddy period beyond 4 weeks where both the buddy and new starter feel this would be helpful.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where no suitable experienced staff member is available at a small site, the registered manager arranges a buddy from a neighbouring site for informal telephone or message support; since assignment is now mandatory, the absence of an obvious on-site buddy is no longer treated as grounds to skip the scheme entirely.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the New Starter Induction Programme Outline (the formal induction this scheme complements) and the Staff Supervision and Appraisal Policy (the more formal line management relationship this scheme sits alongside).

Probationary Period Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out the probationary period every new employee serves, and how it is reviewed and confirmed. It applies to every new starter, and to any existing employee moving into a new role that Alderbridge treats as requiring a fresh probationary assessment.

Policy statement

Probation is a genuine, two-way assessment period: Alderbridge assesses whether the new starter is settling well and meeting the role's requirements, and the new starter assesses whether the role and Alderbridge are right for them, with support and honest feedback flowing in both directions throughout.

Definitions

**Probationary period** the standard 6-month period from an employee's start date during which suitability is formally assessed. **Extension** an additional period, up to 3 months, added where more time is genuinely needed to reach a fair decision. **Probation review** a scheduled formal conversation reviewing progress against the role's requirements.

Roles and responsibilities

**The line manager** holds regular informal check-ins and every formal review, raising any concern as soon as it arises rather than saving it for a scheduled review. **HR** confirms the outcome of each formal review in writing and advises on any complex case. **The new starter** engages openly with feedback and raises any concern about their own induction or support.

The probationary period runs for 6 months from the start date, extendable by up to a further 3 months at the registered manager's discretion where more time is needed.

Formal review meetings are held at 6 weeks, 3 months and 5 months, each recorded in writing.

Any conduct, capability or attendance concern is raised with the employee as soon as it arises, not held back until the next scheduled review.

Successful completion of probation is confirmed to the employee in writing, normally by the end of the 6-month period.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates how the amber trigger point is used supportively rather than punitively. A care worker at Harbour View reaches the amber trigger point after three short, apparently unconnected absences (a stomach bug, a migraine, and a dental abscess) within eight months. At the return-to-work discussion following the third absence, the line manager raises the pattern gently, asks whether anything at work might be contributing, and learns that recent long shifts without an adequate break have been making the employee's migraines worse. Rather than treating the trigger as itself the problem, the line manager and employee agree a shift-length adjustment for a trial period, and no formal absence review meeting is needed, because the amber conversation itself surfaced and addressed the underlying issue — exactly the outcome this policy is designed to produce at that stage.

Extended worked example: a sustained absence with an uncertain return date

A second worked example addresses the harder case of long-term sickness absence. An employee at Oakfield Lodge has been absent for 6 weeks following surgery, with the GP's fit note indicating an uncertain return date. HR arranges an occupational health referral at 4 weeks, per the sustained trigger point, and the resulting report suggests a phased return over 4 weeks with modified duties (no manual handling) would be achievable from week 8. The registered manager agrees this phased return plan with the employee, reviewing it fortnightly and adjusting the pace if the employee's own recovery runs ahead of or behind the initial estimate, rather than treating the occupational health report as a fixed, unchangeable timetable regardless of how the employee is actually progressing.

Feedback from the employee's own perspective

Every probation review genuinely invites the employee's own view of how their induction, support and settling-in period has gone, not only the manager's assessment of them, since a probationary period that is not working well sometimes reflects a genuine gap in the support Alderbridge itself provided, which this two-way conversation is specifically designed to surface honestly.

What happens if probation is not confirmed

Where probation is not confirmed, the reasons are explained clearly and in person wherever possible, the employee's outstanding entitlements (unused leave, final pay) are processed promptly, and an exit conversation offers the employee an opportunity to give feedback on their own experience, which HR reviews for any wider induction or support lesson.

Confidentiality during probation reviews

Probation review notes are shared only with those who need them (the employee, their manager, and HR) and are not discussed informally with colleagues, since a probationary employee is entitled to the same basic confidentiality about their own performance conversations as any other employee.

Site-by-site implementation notes

Disciplinary hearings are deliberately held away from the employee's own immediate workplace wherever practicable — for the four care homes and Willow Bank, this typically means using a meeting room at Central Support Office or, where travel is impractical, a private room at a nearby site rather than the employee's own site, to reduce the risk of the hearing itself becoming visible to colleagues or people supported.

Extended worked example: a capability-shaped conduct concern

A worked example illustrates the boundary between conduct and capability. A relatively new care worker at Riverside House has made three separate documentation errors on care records within two months, none individually serious but forming a pattern. Rather than moving straight to a formal disciplinary hearing, the line manager first considers whether this looks like unwillingness (a conduct matter) or a genuine skills gap (a capability matter) — in this example, the employee's own account and the line manager's review of their induction records show they were never given adequate protected time to complete the documentation training module properly. The line manager therefore addresses this initially through additional supervised practice and a revised, individual learning plan rather than the formal disciplinary process, while recording clearly why that judgement was made, so that if the same pattern continues despite that support, the earlier informal period is not treated as if it never happened.

Frequently asked questions

flexible working under this policy?** Yes, a request to reduce hours is one of the specific types of flexible
working this policy covers.

Training and competency

Managers who consider flexible working requests complete training on the statutory framework and the
specific business reasons that can lawfully justify a refusal.

Monitoring and compliance

HR reviews flexible working request outcomes annually across sites, checking for any pattern suggesting
requests from a particular group are approved less often than others, which would warrant closer review.

Record keeping and retention

Flexible working requests and decisions are retained per the Records Retention Schedule.

Flexible working and career progression

A flexible working arrangement never counts against an employee when a promotion or development
opportunity is being considered, and managers are specifically trained to guard against any unconscious
assumption that flexible working signals reduced commitment or ambition, which research consistently
shows is a common and unfair bias affecting flexible workers' career progression.

Purpose and scope

Policy statement

Definitions

Disciplinary hearings are deliberately held away from the employee's own immediate workplace wherever practicable — for the four care homes and Willow Bank, this typically means using a meeting room at Central Support Office or, where travel is impractical, a private room at a nearby site rather than the employee's own site, to reduce the risk of the hearing itself becoming visible to colleagues or people supported.

Extended worked example: a capability-shaped conduct concern

A worked example illustrates the boundary between conduct and capability. A relatively new care worker at Riverside House has made three separate documentation errors on care records within two months, none individually serious but forming a pattern. Rather than moving straight to a formal disciplinary hearing, the line manager first considers whether this looks like unwillingness (a conduct matter) or a genuine skills gap (a capability matter) — in this example, the employee's own account and the line manager's review of their induction records show they were never given adequate protected time to complete the documentation training module properly. The line manager therefore addresses this initially through additional supervised practice and a revised, individual learning plan rather than the formal disciplinary process, while recording clearly why that judgement was made, so that if the same pattern continues despite that support, the earlier informal period is not treated as if it never happened.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates how the amber trigger point is used supportively rather than punitively. A care worker at Harbour View reaches the amber trigger point after three short, apparently unconnected absences (a stomach bug, a migraine, and a dental abscess) within eight months. At the return-to-work discussion following the third absence, the line manager raises the pattern gently, asks whether anything at work might be contributing, and learns that recent long shifts without an adequate break have been making the employee's migraines worse. Rather than treating the trigger as itself the problem, the line manager and employee agree a shift-length adjustment for a trial period, and no formal absence review meeting is needed, because the amber conversation itself surfaced and addressed the underlying issue — exactly the outcome this policy is designed to produce at that stage.

Extended worked example: a sustained absence with an uncertain return date

A second worked example addresses the harder case of long-term sickness absence. An employee at Oakfield Lodge has been absent for 6 weeks following surgery, with the GP's fit note indicating an uncertain return date. HR arranges an occupational health referral at 4 weeks, per the sustained trigger point, and the resulting report suggests a phased return over 4 weeks with modified duties (no manual handling) would be achievable from week 8. The registered manager agrees this phased return plan with the employee, reviewing it fortnightly and adjusting the pace if the employee's own recovery runs ahead of or behind the initial estimate, rather than treating the occupational health report as a fixed, unchangeable timetable regardless of how the employee is actually progressing.

Why the wellbeing and benefits summary was added

A review found a new starter often did not discover the discount scheme or long service recognition scheme until well into their employment, simply because these were documented separately and not consistently introduced during induction; consolidating a summary directly into this handbook ensures every new starter sees the full picture of what Alderbridge offers from their very first day, alongside the more formal contractual terms.

Training and development

Health and safety responsibilities

Site-by-site implementation notes

Disciplinary hearings are deliberately held away from the employee's own immediate workplace wherever practicable — for the four care homes and Willow Bank, this typically means using a meeting room at Central Support Office or, where travel is impractical, a private room at a nearby site rather than the employee's own site, to reduce the risk of the hearing itself becoming visible to colleagues or people supported.

Extended worked example: a capability-shaped conduct concern

A worked example illustrates the boundary between conduct and capability. A relatively new care worker at Riverside House has made three separate documentation errors on care records within two months, none individually serious but forming a pattern. Rather than moving straight to a formal disciplinary hearing, the line manager first considers whether this looks like unwillingness (a conduct matter) or a genuine skills gap (a capability matter) — in this example, the employee's own account and the line manager's review of their induction records show they were never given adequate protected time to complete the documentation training module properly. The line manager therefore addresses this initially through additional supervised practice and a revised, individual learning plan rather than the formal disciplinary process, while recording clearly why that judgement was made, so that if the same pattern continues despite that support, the earlier informal period is not treated as if it never happened.

Feedback from the employee's own perspective

Every probation review genuinely invites the employee's own view of how their induction, support and settling-in period has gone, not only the manager's assessment of them, since a probationary period that is not working well sometimes reflects a genuine gap in the support Alderbridge itself provided, which this two-way conversation is specifically designed to surface honestly.

What happens if probation is not confirmed

Where probation is not confirmed, the reasons are explained clearly and in person wherever possible, the employee's outstanding entitlements (unused leave, final pay) are processed promptly, and an exit conversation offers the employee an opportunity to give feedback on their own experience, which HR reviews for any wider induction or support lesson.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates how the amber trigger point is used supportively rather than punitively. A care worker at Harbour View reaches the amber trigger point after three short, apparently unconnected absences (a stomach bug, a migraine, and a dental abscess) within eight months. At the return-to-work discussion following the third absence, the line manager raises the pattern gently, asks whether anything at work might be contributing, and learns that recent long shifts without an adequate break have been making the employee's migraines worse. Rather than treating the trigger as itself the problem, the line manager and employee agree a shift-length adjustment for a trial period, and no formal absence review meeting is needed, because the amber conversation itself surfaced and addressed the underlying issue — exactly the outcome this policy is designed to produce at that stage.

Extended worked example: a sustained absence with an uncertain return date

A second worked example addresses the harder case of long-term sickness absence. An employee at Oakfield Lodge has been absent for 6 weeks following surgery, with the GP's fit note indicating an uncertain return date. HR arranges an occupational health referral at 4 weeks, per the sustained trigger point, and the resulting report suggests a phased return over 4 weeks with modified duties (no manual handling) would be achievable from week 8. The registered manager agrees this phased return plan with the employee, reviewing it fortnightly and adjusting the pace if the employee's own recovery runs ahead of or behind the initial estimate, rather than treating the occupational health report as a fixed, unchangeable timetable regardless of how the employee is actually progressing.

Probationary Period Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out the probationary period every new employee serves, and how it is reviewed and confirmed. It applies to every new starter, and to any existing employee moving into a new role that Alderbridge treats as requiring a fresh probationary assessment.

Policy statement

Probation is a genuine, two-way assessment period: Alderbridge assesses whether the new starter is settling well and meeting the role's requirements, and the new starter assesses whether the role and Alderbridge are right for them, with support and honest feedback flowing in both directions throughout.

Definitions

**Probationary period** the standard 6-month period from an employee's start date during which suitability is formally assessed. **Extension** an additional period, up to 3 months, added where more time is genuinely needed to reach a fair decision. **Probation review** a scheduled formal conversation reviewing progress against the role's requirements.

Roles and responsibilities

**The line manager** holds regular informal check-ins and every formal review, raising any concern as soon as it arises rather than saving it for a scheduled review. **HR** confirms the outcome of each formal review in writing and advises on any complex case. **The new starter** engages openly with feedback and raises any concern about their own induction or support.

The probationary period runs for 6 months from the start date, extendable by up to a further 3 months at the registered manager's discretion where more time is needed.

Formal review meetings are held at 6 weeks, 3 months and 5 months, each recorded in writing.

Any conduct, capability or attendance concern is raised with the employee as soon as it arises, not held back until the next scheduled review.

Successful completion of probation is confirmed to the employee in writing, normally by the end of the 6-month period.

Successful completion of probation is confirmed to the employee in writing, normally by the end of the 6-month period.

Where performance or conduct concerns cannot be resolved, employment may be ended with the applicable statutory or contractual notice, whichever is greater, without the full Disciplinary Procedure applying during probation.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a probationary employee's absence pattern reaches a Sickness Absence Policy trigger point, the line manager and HR consider the specific circumstances (for example, a short-term illness clearly unrelated to any underlying concern) before deciding whether this affects the probation outcome, rather than applying a mechanical rule regardless of context.

Local and regional variations

No local or regional variation applies; the probationary period and review structure are identical at every site.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy works alongside the New Starter Onboarding Checklist and Induction Buddy Scheme Guidance for the practical support structure during probation, and the Sickness Absence Policy for how absence during probation is handled.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates an extension used constructively. A new care worker at Moorland View shows promise but has not yet completed all mandatory training by the 5-month review due to a training provider's own scheduling delay, through no fault of the employee. The registered manager extends probation by 6 weeks specifically to allow the outstanding training to be completed and properly assessed, rather than making a premature decision based on an incomplete picture.

Frequently asked questions

**Can probation be confirmed early, before 6 months?** Yes, where a manager is confident the standard has clearly been met, probation may be confirmed early with HR's agreement. **What support is available if I'm struggling during probation?** Raise it with your line manager as early as possible; additional supervised practice, a revised learning plan, or occupational health referral are all considered depending on the nature of the difficulty. **Does a probationary employee have the same rights as a confirmed employee?** Yes to the same core employment rights, though the process for ending employment during probation is simpler, as this policy describes.

Induction Buddy Scheme Guidance

*Supersedes the version effective 1 September 2025. 'Should' becomes 'must' — the buddy assignment is no longer discretionary.*

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the induction buddy scheme offered to a new starter at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every new starter across every site.

Policy statement

New starters must be assigned an experienced buddy for their first 4 weeks — no longer discretionary — giving every new starter an approachable, informal point of contact alongside their formal induction programme.

Definitions

**Buddy** an experienced staff member paired with a new starter to offer informal support and answer day-to-day questions. **Buddy period** the first 4 weeks of a new starter's employment, during which the buddy pairing is now mandatory.

1. Identify a suitable experienced staff member as a buddy before the new starter's first day; this assignment is now mandatory rather than discretionary as under the previous version.
2. Introduce the buddy to the new starter on their first day, explaining the buddy's role as an informal, approachable point of contact.
3. Check in with both the buddy and the new starter partway through the 4-week period to see how the pairing is working.
4. Extend the buddy period beyond 4 weeks where both the buddy and new starter feel this would be helpful.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where no suitable experienced staff member is available at a small site, the registered manager arranges a buddy from a neighbouring site for informal telephone or message support; since assignment is now mandatory, the absence of an obvious on-site buddy is no longer treated as grounds to skip the scheme entirely.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the New Starter Induction Programme Outline (the formal induction this scheme complements) and the Staff Supervision and Appraisal Policy (the more formal line management relationship this scheme sits alongside).

What a formal absence review meeting actually covers

A formal absence review meeting triggered at the red level is a genuinely two-way conversation, not a predetermined disciplinary step: it reviews the specific pattern openly, explores whether an underlying cause (health, workplace factors, or personal circumstances) can be identified and addressed, considers whether occupational health input would help, and only where a pattern is not disability-related and shows no sign of improving despite support does it begin to move toward considering whether continued employment in the current role remains sustainable — a possibility discussed transparently rather than left unspoken while informally already decided.

Confidentiality of health information disclosed during absence management

Any health information an employee shares as part of a return-to-work discussion or a formal absence review is treated as confidential, shared only with those who genuinely need to know (for example, HR and, where a reasonable adjustment is agreed, the employee's own line manager) rather than discussed more widely, and an employee is never expected to disclose more clinical detail than they are comfortable sharing beyond what a fit note or occupational health report already confirms.

Absence during a probationary period

A probationary employee's absence is monitored against the same trigger points, but the shorter probationary window means HR and the line manager review any absence pattern more promptly, since a genuine, sustained concern about attendance reliability is relevant to the eventual probation confirmation decision under the Probationary Period Policy, discussed openly with the employee rather than left unaddressed until the probation end date arrives.

Closing note on tone

Every conversation this policy describes — a return-to-work discussion, an absence review, a trigger-point escalation — is expected to be conducted with genuine warmth and curiosity about what is actually going on for the employee, since a policy applied correctly but coldly achieves compliance without achieving the actual purpose this policy exists for, which is a workplace where people feel able to be honest about being unwell and supported back when they are ready.

flagged as an overdue action at the next Health and Safety Committee and completed as a priority, not
deferred to the next routine review cycle. **Do visitors need to be told the evacuation procedure?** Visitors
are asked to follow staff instruction during an evacuation rather than being separately trained; reception
briefly explains the assembly point location as part of sign-in. **What happens if a fire drill reveals an

Induction Buddy Scheme Guidance

*Supersedes the version effective 1 September 2025. 'Should' becomes 'must' — the buddy assignment is no longer discretionary.*

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the induction buddy scheme offered to a new starter at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every new starter across every site.

Policy statement

New starters must be assigned an experienced buddy for their first 4 weeks — no longer discretionary — giving every new starter an approachable, informal point of contact alongside their formal induction programme.

Definitions

**Buddy** an experienced staff member paired with a new starter to offer informal support and answer day-to-day questions. **Buddy period** the first 4 weeks of a new starter's employment, during which the buddy pairing is now mandatory.

1. Identify a suitable experienced staff member as a buddy before the new starter's first day; this assignment is now mandatory rather than discretionary as under the previous version.
2. Introduce the buddy to the new starter on their first day, explaining the buddy's role as an informal, approachable point of contact.
3. Check in with both the buddy and the new starter partway through the 4-week period to see how the pairing is working.
4. Extend the buddy period beyond 4 weeks where both the buddy and new starter feel this would be helpful.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where no suitable experienced staff member is available at a small site, the registered manager arranges a buddy from a neighbouring site for informal telephone or message support; since assignment is now mandatory, the absence of an obvious on-site buddy is no longer treated as grounds to skip the scheme entirely.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the New Starter Induction Programme Outline (the formal induction this scheme complements) and the Staff Supervision and Appraisal Policy (the more formal line management relationship this scheme sits alongside).

Worked example

Leave and absence

Annual leave entitlement is set out in each employee's own contract and requested through the standard leave request process; sickness absence is reported to the registered manager as early as possible on the first day of absence, now with a wellbeing check-in offered as part of the return-to-work process.

Standards of conduct

Every employee is expected to treat a resident, colleague, and visitor with dignity and respect at all times, to act within the boundaries of their own training and competence, and to raise a concern honestly rather than conceal it.

Health and safety responsibilities

Every employee has a personal responsibility to work safely, to report a hazard or near-miss promptly, and to follow the specific safety procedure relevant to their role; the Health and Safety Policy (Full Manual) sets out the complete framework.

Safeguarding responsibilities

Every employee has a personal responsibility to report a safeguarding concern immediately to their registered manager, following the Adult Safeguarding Policy.

Equality, diversity and inclusion

Alderbridge is committed to treating every employee and resident fairly regardless of a protected characteristic; a concern about discrimination or unfair treatment is raised with Human Resources and taken seriously.

Confidentiality and data protection

An employee has access to confidential information about a resident, a colleague, or Alderbridge's own business in the course of their role; this information is shared only on a need-to-know basis and never disclosed outside of work.

Use of Alderbridge equipment and systems

Alderbridge equipment is provided for legitimate work purposes; reasonable personal use of a shared computer is generally acceptable where it does not interfere with work or breach confidentiality.

Grievance and dispute resolution

Where an employee has a concern about their treatment at work, they are encouraged to raise it informally with their registered manager in the first instance; where this does not resolve the matter, the formal Grievance Procedure sets out the full process.

Training and development

Every employee completes mandatory training relevant to their role as part of induction and on an ongoing refresher basis; a development conversation takes place at least annually as part of the appraisal process.

Uniform and appearance

Where a role requires a uniform, this is provided by Alderbridge and is expected to be worn clean and in good repair; general appearance standards are set out in the Dress and Appearance Guidance.

The individual moving and handling risk assessment in detail

Every MHRA records, at minimum, the person's current weight-bearing ability, their level of cooperation and understanding of what is being asked of them, the specific equipment required (including sling size and hoist type where relevant), the number of staff required, any specific technique variation (for example, a preferred side to approach from following a stroke), and the date of the last review; a care worker unfamiliar with a person for the first time (for example, covering an unfamiliar shift) is expected to read the full MHRA before providing any assistance, not only a summary or a colleague's verbal description of what is normally done.

When an MHRA needs an urgent, unscheduled review

An MHRA is reviewed immediately, not at the next routine 6-month point, following any fall, any hospital admission, any surgery, or any other event that could plausibly have changed a person's mobility, strength, or cooperation; the registered manager is responsible for identifying when such a trigger has occurred and ensuring the review happens before the person is next assisted to move, even where this means a temporary, more cautious default technique is used in the interim while the full review is arranged.

Bariatric and specialist equipment needs

Where a person's weight or body shape means standard equipment is not suitable, a specialist bariatric assessment is arranged, specifying bariatric-rated hoists, slings and, where needed, wider doorways or reinforced flooring; this assessment is treated with particular care and dignity, discussed sensitively with the person and their family, and reviewed by the Health and Safety Lead directly rather than left solely to the site's own moving and handling champion given the additional equipment and structural considerations involved.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Absence wholly attributable to a disability within the meaning of the Equality Act 2010, or to pregnancy-related illness occurring in the two weeks following childbirth, is disregarded when calculating whether a trigger point has been reached, reflecting Alderbridge's legal obligation not to treat a disability-related absence the same as an unrelated one for this purpose. Local and regional variations

No local or regional variation applies to the reporting timescale or trigger points themselves, which are deliberately standardised; what does vary by site is the specific staffing-cover arrangement a registered manager puts in place for a given absence, since a Willow Bank community visit gap is covered differently in practice from a residential shift gap, even though the underlying reporting and review process is identical.

All staff complete equality, dignity and respect training at induction and refresher training every 2 years, and managers complete additional training on handling a discrimination or harassment complaint fairly.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

Extended worked example: a reasonable adjustment for a resident

A worked example illustrates that this policy's dignity commitment applies to people supported, not only staff. A resident at Riverside House living with a visual impairment finds it increasingly difficult to identify her own room among several similar doors on her corridor. Rather than treating this as an inevitable consequence of her condition, staff introduce a simple, high-contrast tactile marker on her door, chosen together with her rather than imposed, and the change is recorded in her care plan as a reasonable adjustment. The registered manager subsequently reviews whether other residents on the same corridor might benefit from a similar approach, rather than treating the adjustment as a one-off fix specific to a single request.

What a formal absence review meeting actually covers

A formal absence review meeting triggered at the red level is a genuinely two-way conversation, not a predetermined disciplinary step: it reviews the specific pattern openly, explores whether an underlying cause (health, workplace factors, or personal circumstances) can be identified and addressed, considers whether occupational health input would help, and only where a pattern is not disability-related and shows no sign of improving despite support does it begin to move toward considering whether continued employment in the current role remains sustainable — a possibility discussed transparently rather than left unspoken while informally already decided.

Confidentiality of health information disclosed during absence management

Any health information an employee shares as part of a return-to-work discussion or a formal absence review is treated as confidential, shared only with those who genuinely need to know (for example, HR and, where a reasonable adjustment is agreed, the employee's own line manager) rather than discussed more widely, and an employee is never expected to disclose more clinical detail than they are comfortable sharing beyond what a fit note or occupational health report already confirms.

Absence during a probationary period

A probationary employee's absence is monitored against the same trigger points, but the shorter probationary window means HR and the line manager review any absence pattern more promptly, since a genuine, sustained concern about attendance reliability is relevant to the eventual probation confirmation decision under the Probationary Period Policy, discussed openly with the employee rather than left unaddressed until the probation end date arrives.

Closing note on tone

Every conversation this policy describes — a return-to-work discussion, an absence review, a trigger-point escalation — is expected to be conducted with genuine warmth and curiosity about what is actually going on for the employee, since a policy applied correctly but coldly achieves compliance without achieving the actual purpose this policy exists for, which is a workplace where people feel able to be honest about being unwell and supported back when they are ready.

Conduct at social events and outside work

Where staff attend an Alderbridge-organised social event, the same fundamental standards of respect and appropriate behaviour apply, though the specific dress code and formality of the workplace itself is relaxed; conduct that would be a disciplinary matter at work (harassment, discrimination) remains exactly as serious at a work social event, since the change of setting does not change the underlying standard expected.

Personal relationships between colleagues

A personal relationship between two colleagues is not itself prohibited, but where one holds a direct managerial or supervisory relationship over the other, this is disclosed to HR so that any potential conflict of interest — for example, in a performance review, a shift allocation decision, or a disciplinary matter — can be managed transparently, protecting both individuals and the fairness of the process for everyone else involved.

Conduct expectations around confidentiality of care information

Beyond the general confidentiality expectation stated earlier, staff are specifically reminded that information about a person supported's health, behaviour or personal circumstances is shared only on a genuine need-to-know basis even within the team, since casual staff-room discussion of a resident's private affairs is a real and recurring risk this section is written to explicitly discourage, not merely a theoretical concern.

Conduct towards contractors and external professionals

Staff extend the same courtesy and professionalism to contractors, visiting healthcare professionals and inspectors as to colleagues and residents, recognising that these interactions also shape how Alderbridge is perceived externally and that a defensive or unhelpful attitude toward, for example, a CQC inspector reflects poorly on the whole organisation regardless of any individual's personal view of a specific visit.

Use of alcohol and substances

Staff do not attend work under the influence of alcohol or any substance affecting their ability to work safely, and any such concern is raised with the registered manager immediately given the direct safety implications in a care environment; occasional moderate alcohol consumption at an evening work social event, where staff are not on duty or on call, is a separate matter handled with ordinary common sense.

Reviewing an ongoing flexible arrangement

An established flexible working arrangement is reviewed periodically by mutual agreement, particularly

support rather than relying solely on written policy guidance for a genuinely new and sometimes finely

Flexible working, handled well, is one of the clearest practical demonstrations of Alderbridge trusting its
